title: How to Bake Sourdough-Based Savory Scones for Tea Time
meta_description: Master savory sourdough tea scones with this easy guide. Learn the best tips for a flaky crust using a sourdough tea scones silicone mat for easy cleanup.
html:
There is something uniquely satisfying about using a sourdough discard to create a savory treat. While most people associate tea time with sweet jam and clotted cream, a savory scone—packed with sharp cheddar and fresh herbs—is the perfect companion for a pot of Earl Grey or a crisp glass of cider. The secret to that professional, golden-bottom crust is using a sourdough tea scones silicone mat, which ensures your buttery dough doesn't stick and bakes evenly across the tray.

Why Use Sourdough Discard for Scones?

If you keep a sourdough starter, you know the struggle of managing the discard. Using it in scones isn't just about reducing waste; it adds a complex, subtle tang that balances the richness of butter and cheese. Unlike traditional scones that rely solely on baking powder, the acidity in the sourdough reacts with leavening agents to create a lighter, more tender crumb.

Because scone dough is high in fat, it can sometimes slump or stick to the pan. This is where Silicone Baking Mats come into play. By replacing parchment paper, these mats provide a consistent heat distribution that prevents the bottoms of your scones from burning while the tops are still pale.

Ingredients for Savory Sourdough Scones

For the best results, keep your butter cold. Cold butter creates small pockets of steam in the oven, which is what gives you those coveted flaky layers.

  • 2 cups all-purpose flour
  • 1 tablespoon baking powder
  • 1/2 teaspoon salt
  • 1/2 cup cold unsalted butter, cubed
  • 1 cup sharp cheddar cheese, shredded
  • 2 tablespoons fresh chives or rosemary, minced
  • 1/2 cup sourdough discard (unfed)
  • 1/4 cup heavy cream or buttermilk (adjust based on discard consistency)
  • 1 egg (for egg wash)

The Step-by-Step Baking Process

Start by preheating your oven to 400°F. Line your baking sheet with Silicone Baking Mats. This is the most important prep step because savory scones—especially those with cheese—tend to leak oil and proteins that can glue themselves to a metal pan.

In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, and salt. Use a pastry cutter or your fingers to work the cold butter into the flour until it looks like coarse crumbs. Stir in the shredded cheese and minced herbs.

Fold in the sourdough discard. Depending on how hydrated your starter is, you may need to add the heavy cream a tablespoon at a time. The dough should be shaggy and just hold together; if you overwork it, your scones will be tough rather than tender.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and pat it into a 1-inch thick circle. Cut the circle into 8 wedges. Place them on your sourdough tea scones silicone mat, leaving about an inch of space between each piece to allow for expansion.

Achieving the Perfect Golden Crust

To get that bakery-style finish, whisk one egg with a splash of water and brush it generously over the top of each scone. This creates a glossy, deep golden brown exterior that contrasts beautifully with the soft interior.

Bake for 18 to 22 minutes. Because you are using Silicone Baking Mats, you don't have to worry about the cheese caramelizing and sticking to the pan. The non-stick surface allows the scones to slide right off the moment they leave the oven, meaning no scrubbing the baking sheet afterward.

Serving and Storage Tips

Savory scones are best served warm. If you aren't eating them immediately, let them cool completely on a wire rack before storing them in an airtight container. They will stay fresh for about three days at room temperature.

To revive them, pop a scone in the toaster oven for two minutes. This brings back the crisp edges and melts the cheese once more. Pair them with a side of salted butter or a dollop of cream cheese for a truly indulgent tea-time experience.

FAQ

Can I freeze sourdough scones?

Yes. You can freeze them after baking and before the final cooling. Once frozen, store them in a freezer bag. Reheat them in the oven at 350°F for about 5-8 minutes to restore the texture.

What if my dough is too sticky to handle?

Sourdough discard varies in thickness. If the dough is too wet, add more flour one tablespoon at a time. Remember that a slightly sticky dough often leads to a more tender scone, so avoid adding too much extra flour.

Do I really need a silicone mat instead of parchment?

While parchment works, Silicone Baking Mats are a more sustainable, reusable option that offers superior heat distribution. They prevent the "hot spots" often found on metal pans, ensuring every scone is baked evenly without the waste of single-use paper.
